prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: I keep B015 as a single-part prize, and after reading the whole first round and the chair's questions I hold it more firmly than before. The reason is the physics, not the count of supporters. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the lattice light shift for the clock transition, so a large ensemble of atoms can be interrogated with essentially no perturbation of the transition. That is a controlled many-atom quantum system, and it is what later made spin-exchange and correlated-clock physics and millimetre-scale gravitational-redshift measurements possible. Ye's group then showed the idea could be taken to the 10^-18 level with every systematic (blackbody shift, hyperpolarisability, collisions) identified and measured. Independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL) with Sr, Yb and Hg compare clocks at that level, which is the robustness test I apply as a theorist working beside experimentalists. On the chair's question about distinctness, I think the 2005 comb prize rewarded the means of counting optical cycles and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single ions, whereas the lattice clock is a different principle: many atoms, a lattice that does not shift the transition, and a new route to many-body metrology. On citation wording, I would name the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 level and say nothing that implies lattice clocks alone define timekeeping, since Al+ and Yb+ ion clocks compete. On the SI second, I would not let the redefinition timetable decide anything; the scientific record is already sufficient, and the redefinition is a metrological decision downstream of it. I am changing nothing in the configuration from round 1, but I am narrowing my reasons.
statement.case_against: The honest objection is that the discovery content is smaller than the instrument content: this is invention and extraordinary refinement of recognised tools more than a surprise about nature, and a committee that weights surprise (a new phase of matter in B003, a new window in B014) can reasonably prefer those. The credit pair is not the whole history: Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko and the ion-clock groups (Wineland, Rosenband, Schmidt) have real claims, and Ye's contribution partly rests on combs and ultrastable cavities built by others. My answer is that the pair is defined by the two distinct achievements, the concept with the first demonstration (Katori) and the extension to the 10^-18 regime and many-body clocks (Ye), and that a narrow citation keeps the boundary defensible. I admit that the boundary is a judgement, not a proof. I also note that several of us who support B015 say that our support rests partly on its clean attribution and broad ranking; that is not an independent scientific argument, and I am not relying on it.

responses.point: Lindroth warns that a clock citation must not suggest that lattice clocks alone define the state of the art, since ion clocks (Al+, Yb+) compete at similar accuracy, and she concedes that the case is one of invention and measurement rather than surprise.
responses.response: I accept the platform-neutrality point and have written my citation so that it credits the magic-wavelength lattice concept and the 10^-18 level of optical frequency standards rather than 'the' state of the art in timekeeping. I would go slightly further than your concession: the lattice clock is not only a precision gain, it creates a regime where a million-atom sample is a controlled many-body quantum system, and that is the part that ion clocks, with one or a few ions, do not provide. That is my answer to the discovery versus refinement objection. I would still say plainly that it is not a surprise in the sense that a new phase of matter is, and I think the committee should accept that and decide whether it is enough.

responses.point: Kroll supports B015 as a measurement advance that changes what can be measured, and flags the pending SI second redefinition and his own year in John Hall's laboratory as relevant to Ye's training.
responses.response: I read your Hall-laboratory link as a disclosure that does not bear on the physics, since you report no collaboration with Katori or Ye, and I would not ask you to step back from B015. On timing, I disagree with using the redefinition as a reason either to act or to wait. If the second is redefined, that follows from the clocks already working; if it slips, the 10^-18 comparisons between laboratories are still true. I would ask that the committee record that the prize rests on the science and that I do not want the redefinition mentioned in the citation. I also take your earlier point about the ion experiments in B009 and see why you place it ahead of circuit QED.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps IceCube (B014) first as a discovery made by nature, the diffuse flux and TXS 0506+056, while conceding that B015 is easier to defend and that attribution among Halzen, Karle, AMANDA and the collaboration is the hard part.
responses.response: I value your framing that nature handed us the flux, and I have no doubt that it is established. This is where I defer to you and Mark on the astroparticle side. My difficulty remains the one you name yourself: two names from a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA, DUMAND, Baikal and ANTARES behind them, and the origin of most of the flux still open. If you can give a citation that rests on the diffuse flux alone and name the two people without leaving a real injustice, I would move B014 above B003 in my alternatives. Without that I do not think it can be the lead this year. I do not take the 'discovery made by nature' argument as stronger than the clock case just because the clock was made by people.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B003 (Kane, Molenkamp, Xue) as a complete theory-experiment arc with more than fifteen years of independent confirmation, but concedes that it omits Mele, Hasan and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, that QSH and QAH are separate experiments, and that weighing it against B015 is not settled for him.
responses.response: I think your description of the maturity is correct, and B003 stays my first alternative. The scientific quality is not what separates it from B015 for me. What separates them is the credit: Mele is the co-author of the Kane-Mele paper, Hasan led the three-dimensional work, and BHZ made the HgTe experiment possible with Zhang deceased, so a three-name cut cannot avoid leaving out someone whose contribution a specialist would call essential. I would prefer a Kane and Molenkamp citation to the compound B003 bundle if the committee turns to condensed matter, but you know the field better than I do and I would follow your judgement on whether Xue's QAH belongs in the same prize.

responses.point: Mehlig supports B015 because the magic-wavelength idea is a clean mechanism that was then confirmed at extreme precision, but states that it is an instrument achievement more than a new principle of nature and that it sits beside the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree with the mechanism argument, and I accept that it is an instrument achievement. The 2005 and 2012 prizes are where I part from the objection: neither covered a lattice that cancels the light shift or the many-atom interrogation that follows, so I treat the overlap as limited, and I agree that this needs to be said explicitly in the deliberation. I would not exchange it for B005. Fluctuation theorems may be a deeper, more universal statement, but the credit among Jarzynski, Evans, Crooks, Gallavotti, Cohen, Kurchan and others is not settled for the three-name cap, and I do not think a prize should be given where the committee cannot name the people with confidence.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will read the lattice clock as a distinct new regime (many-atom controlled quantum system) or as a refinement of what the 2005 and 2012 prizes recognised.
Whether the boundary of the Katori and Ye pair, leaving out Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko and ion-clock groups, is defensible in the record and in the citation wording.
Whether the pending SI second redefinition should affect timing; my own view is that it should not, but I cannot say what others will weigh.

Whether Danielsson can supply a B014 credit framing that survives the attribution objections, and whether Eriksson would accept a narrower Kane and Molenkamp citation, either of which could change the ranking of my alternatives.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I am Director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and a long-time colleague of Chalmers superconducting-circuit groups, with professional links to the circuit QED community (Schoelkopf, Wallraff, Blais; B039), which I ranked first at opening. I now do not propose B039 either as my preferred part or as an alternative, and I recuse myself from the B039 deliberation and vote. Eva Olsson is my Chalmers colleague and we have no joint work relevant to any shortlisted candidate. I have no documented link to Katori or Ye (B015), to the topological-insulator candidates, or to B009, and I do not think any member's disclosed link to B015 requires them to step back.
